sections.title: How does the Warp speed calculator work?
sections.html:
The Warp speed calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports speed (TOS: The Original Series) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the warp factor, the time (TOS: The Original Series), the time (TNG-1: The Next Generation version 1) and the time (TNG-2: The Next Generation version 2).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Warp speed calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Speed=((warp factor), 3)
Distance=299792458 × time × (((warp factor), 3))
Speed=(((warp factor < 9001 ÷ 1000) ? ( (warp factor ^ 10 ÷ 3) ) : ( (warp factor, (3658749373 ÷ 100000000000) × (-the natural log of (10 − warp factor), 4488073677 ÷ 2500000000) ÷ the exponential of ((1 ÷ 1000) ÷ ((warp factor ^ 2) − 18 × warp factor + 81)) + 10 ÷ 3) )))
Distance=299792458 × time × ((((warp factor < 9001 ÷ 1000) ? ( (warp factor ^ 10 ÷ 3) ) : ( (warp factor, (3658749373 ÷ 100000000000) × (-the natural log of (10 − warp factor), 4488073677 ÷ 2500000000) ÷ the exponential of ((1 ÷ 1000) ÷ ((warp factor ^ 2) − 18 × warp factor + 81)) + 10 ÷ 3) ))))
Speed=(((warp factor < 9001 ÷ 1000) ? ( (warp factor ^ 10 ÷ 3) ) : ( (warp factor, (413 ÷ 156250) × (-the natural log of (10 − warp factor), 2879267 ÷ 1000000) + (162873 ÷ 500000) × (warp factor − 9 ^ 11) + (156853 ÷ 2500000) × (warp factor − 9 ^ 5) + 10 ÷ 3) )))
Distance=299792458 × time × ((((warp factor < 9001 ÷ 1000) ? ( (warp factor ^ 10 ÷ 3) ) : ( (warp factor, (413 ÷ 156250) × (-the natural log of (10 − warp factor), 2879267 ÷ 1000000) + (162873 ÷ 500000) × (warp factor − 9 ^ 11) + (156853 ÷ 2500000) × (warp factor − 9 ^ 5) + 10 ÷ 3) ))))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Warp speed calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the warp factor and the time — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Warp speed calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns speed (TOS: The Original Series), derived from the warp factor and the time. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Warp speed calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the warp factor and the time, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance (TOS: The Original Series) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance (TOS: The Original Series) opens in light years and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Speed = 1000. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Warp speed calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
